exercise.name: Resistance Band Bent Over Reverse Fly

reference.title: Resistance Band Bent Over Reverse Fly
reference.listing: Video (movement reference only; the page could not be fetched from the authoring environment (the proxy refused gymvisual.com), so the data sheet was not read; the movement is taken from the exercise name and standard coaching practice)

equipment: Resistance band (two, or one long band under both feet)

breathing.pattern: Breathe out as the arms sweep out, breathe in as they come back down.
breathing.cadence: About 1 s up, short squeeze, about 2 s down

prescription.load: Band tension is user-chosen (bands are colour-coded by tension): pick one you can move for the target reps with 1-3 reps in reserve; step farther from the anchor, or choke up on the band, for more tension.
prescription.progression: More reps, a longer squeeze, a wider stance on the band, then the next band up.

cues.text: Stand on the bands, feet about hip width; hinge at the hips with a flat back until the trunk is well forward, knees soft. Arms hang under the shoulders, palms facing each other, elbows soft.
Breathe out and sweep the arms out to the sides in a wide arc, leading with the elbows, until they are about level with the back.
Squeeze the shoulder blades together; hold the trunk still.
Breathe in and lower the arms back under the shoulders against the band.
Short pause with the band still taut, then sweep again.

mistakes.mistake: Lifting the trunk as the arms rise
mistakes.fix: Hold the hinge; the arms move, the trunk does not.
Hinge from the hips with a flat back; soften the knees more.

mistakes.mistake: Shrugging the shoulders toward the ears
mistakes.fix: Keep the neck long and the shoulders down.

mistakes.mistake: Bending the elbows to row the band up
mistakes.fix: Keep a fixed slight bend and sweep the arms wide.

kinematics.norm: Hinged well forward with a flat back (clinical opinion)
From hanging under the shoulders out to the sides to about level with the back; a neutral grip suits the posterior deltoid (Schoenfeld 2013).
Each band under the ball of its own foot; tension rises toward the top. Elastic resistance can match free weights (Andersen 2010).
About 1 s up and 2 s down (clinical opinion)

sources.title: GymVisual, Resistance Band Bent Over Reverse Fly, video (movement reference)
Schoenfeld et al. 2013, effect of hand position on EMG activity of the posterior shoulder musculature during a horizontal abduction exercise (J Strength Cond Res 27(10):2644-2649)
Campos et al. 2020, different shoulder exercises affect the activation of deltoid portions in resistance-trained individuals (J Hum Kinet 75:5-14)

Andersen, Andersen, Mortensen, Poulsen, Bjornlund and Zebis 2010, muscle activation and perceived loading during rehabilitation exercises: comparison of dumbbells and elastic resistance (Phys Ther 90(4):538-549)

cautions: Check the band for nicks or tears before every session and replace a worn band; a band that snaps can hit the face or eyes.
Anchor the band to something that cannot move or slip (a rack upright, a pull-up bar or under the feet) and make sure it is secure before loading it.
Band tension rises as it stretches, so the load is heaviest at the end of the pull or push; let it return under control rather than snapping back.
Low back: keep the hinge flat-backed and the band light enough that the trunk stays still (clinical opinion).
Keep the band securely under the feet; a band that slips can whip up toward the face.
Stop if sharp pain, numbness or tingling occurs.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
modify: Low back discomfort: do it seated, leaning forward over the thighs, or chest-supported on an incline bench.
progressions: Stronger band or a wider stance on the band.
